findings.title: call_id cannot join pre and post log rows — schema docs claim it can, implementation generates independent values
findings.detail: _call_id() returns int(time.time() * 1_000_000)-{pid}. In the pre-event handler, _call_id() is called at line 179 to write into the temp pair file (but that stored value is never read back — the post handler at line 202 reads only parts[1], the wall-clock timestamp). _call_id() is then called again independently at line 188 to populate the pre-row's call_id field in the payload, producing a different microsecond timestamp. In the post-event handler, a third independent _call_id() call at line 245 generates yet another value for the post-row's call_id. Pre and post rows always carry different call_id values. docs/LOGGING.md line 49 states 'nanosecond ts + PID; matches pre row to its post row' and line 54 states 'pre/post call_id match' — both are false. An agent writing a jq query to correlate pre and post rows by call_id equality will get zero matches. The actual pre/post correlation mechanism is the temp file at pair_path keyed on a sha256 of the tool_input content, used only for timing (duration_ms); there is no call_id-based correlation in the implementation. The precision description is also wrong: the implementation produces microsecond precision, not nanosecond.
findings.recommendation: Capture a single call_id before the pre-event temp file write: assign cid = _call_id() before line 177, write f'{cid} {time.time()}\n' to the temp file (replacing line 179), and use 'call_id': cid in the pre-row payload (replacing line 188). In the post handler, read parts[0] from the temp file and use it as the call_id for the post row (replacing the fresh _call_id() call at line 245 — fall back to _call_id() if the temp file was missing). Update docs/LOGGING.md line 49 to read 'microsecond ts + PID; shared with the matching post row' and remove 'pre/post call_id match' from line 54.

findings.title: Documented redaction extension path directs agents to edit redact.py, which has no effect on live logging
findings.detail: docs/LOGGING.md line 72 says 'If you need to add a pattern, edit hooks/lib/redact.py's _PATTERNS list'. The live logging pipeline is log-tool-calls.sh -> log_tool_call.py. redact.py is not called by log_tool_call.py. Its _PATTERNS are inlined at lines 32-50 of log_tool_call.py with the comment 'kept in sync with hooks/lib/redact.py'. An agent following the documented procedure will edit redact.py, run test-redaction.sh (which exercises redact.py directly and passes), and conclude the new pattern is active. The new pattern will never fire during actual tool call logging because the live path reads from log_tool_call.py's private inlined copy. This is a silent agent failure: the action appeared to succeed (tests pass, no errors) but the goal was not achieved. The Authorization-header partial-leak fix during this PR's own development shows this sync has already been missed once. Related to maintainability M-02, M-03 and testing T-5, but filed here because the agent-native impact is distinct: the documented extension procedure is actively misleading.
findings.recommendation: Update docs/LOGGING.md line 72 to say patterns must be added in BOTH hooks/lib/redact.py AND hooks/lib/log_tool_call.py lines 32-50, until a shared-module approach (maintainability M-02) eliminates the duplication. Add a test that pipes a fixture containing a known secret through 'bash hooks/log-tool-calls.sh pre' and asserts the secret is absent from the JSONL output, exercising log_tool_call.py's patterns independently of redact.py (also recommended by testing T-5).

findings.title: scripts/redact-existing-logs.py is documented as a runnable agent action but does not exist

files.note: directory contains install.sh, statusline.sh, uninstall.sh, validate.sh only

findings.detail: docs/LOGGING.md line 72 says 'To re-redact older logs after adding a pattern, run python3 scripts/redact-existing-logs.py <log-file>'. The scripts/ directory does not contain this file. The spec noted it as 'one-off; not auto-installed' and the plan said 'run manually', but the docs present it as a currently-executable command. An agent following docs to re-redact logs after a pattern change will get 'python3: can\'t open file'. The action is genuinely needed: after a new redaction pattern is added to the live path (per AN-02), there is no tool to retroactively clean up log lines that captured secrets matching the new pattern.
findings.recommendation: Ship the script. It requires only: read the JSONL file line by line, parse each JSON object, apply _PATTERNS (from the shared module after M-02, or imported from log_tool_call.py), re-serialize, write back to the same path. This reuses existing logic and is a low-effort implementation. If the decision is to defer the script, remove the reference from docs/LOGGING.md and replace it with a manual one-liner example, e.g. 'python3 -c "import json,sys,re,pathlib; [...]" ~/.claude/logs/tool-calls-2026-04-01.jsonl'.

findings.title: All logging write failures are silently swallowed with no agent-accessible health diagnostic

files.note: does not check log file recency or directory writability

findings.detail: By design, all logging write failures in log_tool_call.py are swallowed: non-ENOSPC OSErrors fall through to return 0 at line 259; the outer try/except Exception at lines 264-267 catches everything else; set +e in log-tool-calls.sh ensures even a python3 exec failure (e.g., python3 not on PATH) exits 0. This is correct for the never-break-a-tool-call invariant. However, it means an agent has no way to verify that logging is actually working short of directly inspecting a log file and checking its recency. validate.sh confirms that symlinks point correctly and hooks are wired in settings.json, but does not check whether a log line was recently written or whether the log directory is writable. Silent failure scenarios: wrong permissions on ~/.claude/logs/ after a system migration, python3 removed from PATH (reliability R-01 covers the hook exit-code angle; this is about the agent\'s diagnostic view), log_tool_call.py import error due to a broken symlink. An agent that queries the logs for self-analysis after logging has silently stopped will receive empty results with no indication that the data collection infrastructure is broken.
findings.recommendation: Add a log-health check to scripts/validate.sh that verifies: (1) ~/.claude/logs/ exists and is writable (not just that it is a directory), and (2) if a log file for today exists, its mtime is within the last 24 hours; if no log file exists and the session is not new, emit WARN. This is a passive check that does not fire hooks. Alternatively provide scripts/log-health.sh as a standalone diagnostic that an agent can run explicitly when self-analysis queries return unexpectedly sparse results.

what_works_well: JSONL log format is queryable with standard tools — documented schema with field types and six ready-made jq queries in docs/LOGGING.md means agents can write log-analysis queries immediately without schema guessing
MCP tool calls are first-class log citizens: mcp_server is parsed from mcp__<server>__<method> tool names and included on every row, enabling an agent to audit its MCP usage by server

install.sh and uninstall.sh are fully non-interactive and agent-runnable: --dry-run previews all changes, --force handles re-install, component-level granularity (e.g., install.sh hooks) lets an agent update a single subsystem without touching the rest

The global CLAUDE.md template injects runtime infrastructure context directly: log file path pattern, hooks reference path, and logging schema path are stated in the template so agents see them in every session context without needing to discover them
docs/HOOKS.md documents a complete 6-step add-your-own-hook procedure that an agent can follow to extend the safety or logging infrastructure
Redaction is applied to both args and output on every log row before write, so agents reading logs for self-analysis are not exposed to secrets that were present in tool inputs or responses

residual_risks.description: After AN-01 is fixed, agents correlating pre/post rows during high-concurrency sessions (many parallel tool calls with the same tool_input hash) may still see pair-file contention via the fallback glob path in log_tool_call.py lines 211-228. The glob grabs the most-recent temp file matching the session prefix when the exact hash match is absent, which can pair the wrong pre and post rows. This affects duration_ms accuracy but not call_id correctness after the fix. The hash-keyed pairing (non-fallback path) is the robust mechanism.

Even after AN-02 is fixed with updated docs, an agent with a cached or outdated copy of docs/LOGGING.md that only edits redact.py will silently fail to protect the live log path. The permanent protection requires eliminating the duplication via the shared-module approach (maintainability M-02).

testing_gaps.description: No test asserts that pre and post rows for the same tool invocation share a call_id after AN-01 is fixed. Required test: fire pre, capture call_id from the logged line, fire post with the same tool_input, assert the post row's call_id equals the pre row's call_id.

No test verifies that log_tool_call.py's inlined redaction patterns work correctly end-to-end (this is also testing T-5). After AN-02 is fixed, a test piping a secret-bearing fixture through 'bash hooks/log-tool-calls.sh pre' and asserting the secret is absent from the JSONL output is required to prevent silent redaction drift.

Once scripts/redact-existing-logs.py is shipped per AN-03, add a test that creates a JSONL file with a secret-containing line, runs the script, and asserts the secret is replaced by a redaction marker in the output file.

No test verifies that scripts/validate.sh correctly detects a broken logging setup (e.g., a non-writable ~/.claude/logs/ directory or a stale/missing log file). After AN-04 is addressed with log-health checks in validate.sh, add tests for each new health check condition.
